claims.claim: Aramini reports as general critical consensus that Wolfe leaves certain resolutions out of the text for the reader to infer.
claims.source: Marc Anthony Aramini, 'Does It Mean? Gene Wolfe: Perverse Puzzle Maker', PhD dissertation, University of Nevada Las Vegas, May 2019
claims.quote: Wolfe leaves out certain resolutions which are left to the reader

claims.claim: Aramini reports Peter Wright's contrary position that many details in Wolfe's primary narrative are distractions rather than clues.
claims.source: Peter Wright, Attending Daedalus (Liverpool University Press, 2003), summarised by Marc Aramini in his UNLV dissertation, 2019
claims.quote: many of the details included in the primary narrative

claims.claim: Aramini reports Wright's finding that Wolfe's translator persona makes deliberate mistranslations and substitutions inside the Latro books.
claims.source: Peter Wright, Attending Daedalus (Liverpool University Press, 2003), p. 188, quoted by Marc Aramini in his UNLV dissertation, 2019
claims.quote: explicit mistranslations and substitutions by the translator Wolfe

claims.claim: A passage of Wolfe's own fiction reproduced in Aramini's dissertation states that what is not said can be important but what is said matters more.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, The Sword of the Lictor, p. 182, quoted within Peter Wright's argument as reproduced in Marc Aramini's UNLV dissertation, 2019
claims.quote: What is not said can be important

claims.claim: Aramini argues that Wolfe builds his Latro narrative on the Herodotean model of an account that blends history, myth and rumour.
claims.source: Marc Anthony Aramini, UNLV dissertation, May 2019

claims.claim: A passage of Wolfe's The Wizard Knight reproduced in Aramini's dissertation describes a past that survives only as memories and as records nobody reads or can read.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, The Wizard Knight, p. 39, quoted in Marc Aramini's UNLV dissertation, 2019
claims.quote: records nobody reads, and records nobody can read

claims.claim: Clute reports that the large cast of The Book of the Short Sun speaks in dozens of distinct dialects and accents, each rendered with care.
claims.source: John Clute, 'It Is Becoming to Grapple with This Book', Excessive Candour column, Science Fiction Weekly issue 197, 29 January 2001
claims.quote: dozens of different dialects and accents spoken by the huge cast

claims.claim: Clute identifies Wolfe's refusal to restate a difficult story in easy terms as one of the things the reader must struggle with.
claims.source: John Clute, Science Fiction Weekly issue 197, 29 January 2001
claims.quote: refusal to unpack in easy terms

claims.claim: Clute locates the moral quality of Wolfe's central character in the details rather than in any statement about him.
claims.source: John Clute, Science Fiction Weekly issue 197, 29 January 2001
claims.quote: that goodness is in the details

claims.claim: Clute argues that every word in Wolfe's stories is deliberate, so that no sentence can be slurred over by the reader.
claims.source: John Clute, review of The Best of Gene Wolfe, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: every word he wrote was meant

claims.claim: Clute states that Wolfe did not write metaphors into his text, or wrote only metaphors to which a literal meaning could be attached.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: Wolfe did not create metaphors in his text

claims.claim: Clute says the nearest Wolfe normally comes to metaphor is letting one of his characters tell a lie.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: the closest Wolfe normally gets to metaphor is when he
claims.page: paragraph on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

claims.claim: Clute argues Wolfe wrote neither thematics nor allegory but the thing itself.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: he did not write allegory, he wrote the thing itself

claims.claim: Clute says Wolfe's stories cannot be paraphrased for meaning because they only make sense once the manner of their telling is understood.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: stories that only make sense when it is understood how

claims.claim: Clute describes the surface of The Fifth Head of Cerberus as a fluent and seemingly translucent style.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: written in a fluent, seemingly translucent style
claims.page: paragraph on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe leaves out certain resolutions which are left to the reader to infer
verdicts.note: Aramini, Introduction (p.7-8 of the PDF text): 'this absence certainly does resonate with the general consensus that Wolfe leaves out certain resolutions which are left to the reader to infer.' Quote verbatim; 'general critical consensus' limb supported by the words 'the general consensus'.

verdicts.trueWording: Wright insists many primary-narrative details are actually distractions
verdicts.note: Same Introduction passage: 'However, Wright insists that many of the details included in the primary narrative in Wolfe's fiction are somehow actually distractions'. Quote verbatim; the 'contrary' limb is carried by 'However', and 'rather than clues' by the quoted Wright text calling the allusions 'largely external to the text and of little use to an understanding of the narrative' and by Aramini's earlier 'distractions and misdirections'.

verdicts.trueWording: explicit mistranslations and substitutions by the translator Wolfe
verdicts.note: Latro chapter (PDF text ~p.41): 'He also notes that these explicit mistranslations and substitutions by the translator Wolfe "[draw] attention to the gap between the signifier and what is signified..." (188).' Quote verbatim, attributed to Wright at p.188 as the claim states; the page's adjective is 'explicit' where the claim says 'deliberate' — same substance (Wolfe writing as the scrolls' translator, with Soldier in the Mist p. xi cited just above).

verdicts.trueWording: What is not said can be important -- but what is said is more important
verdicts.note: Inside the block quotation from Wright: 'What is not said can be important -- but what is said is more important. (Sword, p. 182)'. Quote verbatim and the Sword of the Lictor p.182 citation is on the page. Location note only: the passage sits in the dissertation's Introduction, not a separate 'chapter on critical reception'.

verdicts.trueWording: Herodotus's account blends history, myth, and rumor; Wolfe takes much the same approach
verdicts.note: Latro chapter (~p.65): 'the approach Herodotus takes to his historical account blends history, myth, and rumor, even tying the war with Persia into the oral tradition of Homer, and Wolfe seems to take much the same approach in forging Latro's story.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the past is only memories, and records nobody reads, and records nobody can read
verdicts.note: Quoted from The Knight (volume one of The Wizard Knight), cited '(39)' after an earlier '(Wolfe, Knight 33)', in the chapter whose next sentences turn to Jung's archetypes. Quote verbatim; 'survives only as memories and records' matches 'the past is only memories, and records nobody reads, and records nobody can read.'

verdicts.trueWording: dozens of different dialects and accents spoken by the huge cast, all meticulously rendered
verdicts.note: Clute 2001, section 'A Complex Yet Rewarding Finish': 'There is much to struggle with--the learnings of Silk; the dozens of different dialects and accents spoken by the huge cast, all meticulously rendered...'. Quote verbatim; 'each rendered with care' is the page's 'all meticulously rendered'.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe's refusal to unpack in easy terms a tale inherently difficult to tell
verdicts.note: Same sentence, inside the list introduced by 'There is much to struggle with--': '...Wolfe's refusal to unpack in easy terms a tale which is inherently difficult to tell'. Quote verbatim; both limbs (the refusal, and its being one of the things to struggle with) are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: we know that Silk is indeed good. And that goodness is in the details
verdicts.note: Quote 'that goodness is in the details' is verbatim in the section 'A Complex Yet Rewarding Finish', and the goodness-in-the-details limb holds. But the page draws no contrast with statement: the same sentence flatly states 'we know that Silk, on the other hand, is indeed good', and the column also quotes Hoof's plain 'Father was good' and Clute's own earlier 'one of the most luminously good figures in 20th century literature'. The 'rather than in any statement about him' limb is the verifier's addition, not Clute's.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: rather than in any statement about him

verdicts.trueWording: every word he wrote was meant; no slurring over of sentences
verdicts.note: Clute 2009, the paragraph on learning to read Wolfe in the 1970s: 'The first thing to understand, I thought then (and now), was that every word he wrote was meant. There could be no slurring over of sentences in the reader's mind.' Quote verbatim; both limbs on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe did not create metaphors in his text -- or only metaphors with a literal meaning attached
verdicts.note: Same paragraph: 'As Wolfe did not create metaphors in his text-or if he only created metaphors to which a literal meaning, a literal architectonic, could be attached-there were no easy copouts for the reader'. Quote verbatim; the claim's disjunction matches the page's.

verdicts.trueWording: the closest Wolfe normally gets to metaphor is when he allows one of his protagonists to tell a lie
verdicts.note: In the Fifth Head of Cerberus paragraph, as the claim's page field says. Quote verbatim. The page says 'one of his protagonists' where the claim says 'one of his characters' — a broadening of the same statement, not a different one.

verdicts.trueWording: he did not write thematics, he did not write allegory, he wrote the thing itself
verdicts.note: 1970s paragraph: '...he did not write thematics, he did not write allegory, he wrote the thing itself.' The claim's quote is a contiguous verbatim substring, and the 'neither thematics nor allegory' limb is the clause immediately before it.

verdicts.trueWording: you cannot abstract themes from stories that only make sense when it is understood how they have been told
verdicts.note: The paragraph on academics shunning Wolfe: 'because you cannot strip-mine Gene Wolfe for "meaning," you cannot abstract themes from stories that only make sense when it is understood how they have been told.' Quote verbatim; the 'cannot be paraphrased for meaning' limb is supported here and by the earlier 'no schizo paraphrasing of what he said into story and meaning'.

verdicts.trueWording: written in a fluent, seemingly translucent style that may distract the reader
verdicts.note: '"The Fifth Head of Cerberus", which is all about guarding (and attempting to escape from) the hell within, is written in a fluent, seemingly translucent style that may distract the reader from realizing that it can only be understood when every word is adhered to literally.' Quote verbatim; 'surface' is fair for a style that 'may distract the reader' from the literal reading beneath it. Clute is describing the novella of that name, the collection's opening story.
